items.title: Apple announces its first touchscreen Mac at the 'Pro and Tell' event — the redesigned 14-inch and 16-inch 'MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display' uses a tandem OLED touch panel (2,000 nits, 120Hz, ~3 lb), M5 Pro and M5 Max chips (up to 128 GB unified memory, 614 GB/s bandwidth), $2,899 / $3,399 starting, pre-orders Oct 28, in-store Nov 6
items.summary: Apple's October 28 'Pro and Tell' invite-only event in Los Angeles produced the first touchscreen Mac. Live-blog coverage during the 10 AM PT event (Macworld, Engadget, T3, TechRadar, Tom's Guide) reports the new product is called 'MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display,' built around a tandem OLED panel at 2,000 nits sustained brightness and a 120Hz refresh, in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes. The chassis is reportedly a redesign — thinner and lighter (~3 lb for the 14-inch), with a Dynamic Island-style camera cutout replacing the notch, and touch positioned as an additional input alongside keyboard and trackpad rather than a replacement. Apple's choice of silicon is the M5 Pro and M5 Max rather than a new M6 Pro/Max — M5 Max tops out at 128 GB of unified memory at 614 GB/s bandwidth, M5 Pro at 64 GB and 307 GB/s. Reported starting prices are $2,899 for the 14-inch and $3,399 for the 16-inch. Pre-orders opened at 10:10 AM PT; retail availability is reported as November 6. Apple did not livestream the event — coverage is from the invited press in LA, so specific line-item configuration prices and the full options matrix are still filtering out. This is a distinct product from the base 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro ($1,999) and 24-inch M6 iMac ($1,499) that Apple announced October 27; the Pro-and-Tell models sit on last-generation Max-class silicon with the new touchscreen OLED panel, while the base M6 line keeps the current non-touch design on the newer 2 nm chip. Earlier Bloomberg reporting that Apple is skipping M6 Pro and M6 Max chips to accelerate M7 development is consistent with today's naming choice but has not been explicitly confirmed by Apple.
items.why_it_matters: The AI-relevant read on this launch is the memory ceiling, not the touchscreen. The M5 Max option carries up to 128 GB of unified memory at 614 GB/s — the single most important spec for running a local LLM on a Mac, because token-generation speed is roughly capped by how fast the chip reads model weights from memory. In practical terms, 128 GB unified memory with macOS's ~75% GPU allocation gives roughly 96 GB of usable model budget, which is the ballpark that puts a 70B-parameter model (quantized) in reach on a laptop and makes larger MoE models runnable. For Gabe's Python stack specifically, this is the machine where `ollama run` or `mlx-lm` on a 70B model becomes a reasonable local-development loop rather than a cloud call — the practical bar between 'I can hobby-code against a local Llama/Qwen/Mistral' and 'I have to pay per token.' The touchscreen itself is more interesting as a software story than a hardware one — Apple adding a touch input to macOS is the UI-framework change that will show up in SwiftUI and AppKit changes, and whatever gestures Apple exposes are the thing a developer would want to design around. The 'MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display' naming (keeping 'MacBook Pro' rather than coining a new product line) is the clearest signal that Apple sees touch as additive to the Mac rather than a sibling product, which is also what Bloomberg's Mark Gurman had reported pre-event. The strategic read, read against yesterday's base-M6 MacBook Pro announcement: Apple is selling two parallel high-end Macs for the next 12+ months — a newer-silicon base MacBook Pro on M6 (no touch, no OLED), and a last-silicon flagship on M5 Max (touch + OLED + the big memory ceiling). The buyer who wants local-LLM headroom pays for the Max; the buyer who wants the newest chip at mainstream pricing takes the M6. Honest caveats: Apple did not livestream the event, and all specifics in this item are from live-blog coverage of the press hands-on in LA. Direct fetches to apple.com, techradar.com, and engadget.com DNS-failed from this agent's egress on this run, so there is no primary-source confirmation here — only consolidated secondary reporting. The $2,899 / $3,399 starting prices were pre-event Bloomberg figures that live-blog coverage repeated during the event, which is weaker than Apple's own newsroom confirmation and should be re-checked once the Apple spec sheet is reachable.
items.why_it_matters_brief: Apple's first touchscreen Mac ships with M5 Max and 128 GB unified memory at 614 GB/s — the memory and bandwidth ceiling that puts a quantized 70B model within reach on a laptop, which is the practical bar for local-LLM Python work on Mac.
